transcript:
Meeting start: 2026-03-21 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Raj (Redwood SE), Hannah (Redwood Solutions), Lina (NorthStar Infra), Mark (NorthStar ML), Olivia (NorthStar Security), James (NorthStar SRE)

Summary:
Quick architectural walkthrough focused on fallback scenarios when Dedicated capacity is saturated, how KV cache hotpaths and batching interact with tail latency, and what guarantees Redwood can provide for throughput/isolation in a VPC/on-prem context. Action items: share tuning docs, run microbenchmarks, plan pilot.

Topics:
- KV cache hotpath behavior and eviction strategies
- Continuous batching vs strict per-req latency SLOs
- Quantization tradeoffs for tail latency and quality
- Routing/fallbacks: model variants, region failover, capacity tiers
- VPC/on-prem constraints and auditability (KMS, audit logs)

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call — state your role and we'll jump in.
[00:07] Lina (Infra): Lina from NorthStar. I'm the infra lead, SRE-ish, focusing on our production latency guarantees.
[00:11] Mark (ML): Mark — ML platform, looking at model serving and KV cache stuff.
[00:15] Olivia (Security): Olivia, security and compliance.
[00:17] James (SRE): James, SRE.
[00:19] Raj (SE): Raj from Redwood, I'll lead the deep-dive.
[00:21] Hannah (Solutions): Hannah, solutions eng.
[00:23] Maya: Cool. Lina, you said you wanted to walk through what happens when dedicated pools hit hot spots and how Redwood's fallback works?
[00:29] Lina: Yeah, exactly. We have bursty payments traffic; sometimes a shard will spike and we get noisy neighbor behavior. We need to understand: will requests queue, failover to hosted, or get throttled? Also KV cache — when it gets hot, eviction seems to blow up p99s.
[00:45] Raj: Great. We'll outline both the runtime behavior and the fallback routing and then talk about tuning: batching window, prefix/KV prefetch, and quantization profiles.

[01:02] Raj: First, dedicated pools are isolated capacity — you have GPUs pinned to your tenant. That reduces noisy neighbor risk but doesn't completely eliminate it: within the pool a single heavy seq-length workload can saturate GPU SMs and memory bandwidth, affecting co-tenants on the same machine if you share instances. We use capacity fencing at the slot level to mitigate that.
[01:25] James: Can you explain capacity fencing? We heard the term but want specifics.
[01:28] Raj: Sure. At a high level, capacity fencing means we allocate whole GPU slots (or soft-affinity slots) to customer workloads and enforce cgroup-level limits on GPU memory and scheduling where supported. If a job tries to exceed its memory, it gets evicted or routed. That prevents memory spill from thrashing other tenants' KV caches.
[01:46] Mark: Does that handle KV cache hotness? Our KV sizes are large; if one tenant's KV cache grows, we see eviction storms.
[01:54] Hannah: Two parts: first, KV cache in our runtime is tenant-scoped by default for Dedicated and can be colocated in GPU DRAM or in a nearby shared NVMe cache depending on configuration. We track access frequency and use an adaptive TTL + LRU-ish eviction, but when you have a sudden hot set beyond GPU capacity, we fall back to NVM and prefetch heuristics can help.
[02:19] Lina: So fallback to NVMe will increase latency spikes, right?
[02:22] Raj: Yes, NVMe fallback increases tail latencies. That's why we have prefetch (read-ahead) heuristics and suggest workload-specific warmup to reduce miss rate. For example, for your payments flows, if you can send KV pre-warm on session start, the p99 drops significantly.
[02:40] Mark: We don't currently pre-warm — would that be part of integration?
[02:43] Maya: That's one of the recommended best practices. We can share a short script to do warmup per user session.

[02:55] [Timestamp jump — 03:00]
[03:00] James: On throughput guarantees — what's realistic? We have business SLAs at p95 120ms and p99 300ms for inference.
[03:07] Raj: For dedicated pools we can hit those SLOs consistently if your workload fits the model and seq-length distribution. The important variables: batch size, continuous batching aggressiveness, KV cache hit-rate, and model variant (quantized vs fp16).
[03:24] Raj: Continuous batching increases throughput but can add wait time to individual requests. We expose batching configuration: max_batch_time_ms and max_batch_tokens. For strict p95 SLOs you might set max_batch_time_ms lower to favor latency at cost of tokens/sec. For throughput SLOs, raise it.
[03:42] Mark: Is there a way to have hybrid — low-latency lane for interactive requests and a high-throughput lane for background workers?
[03:48] Raj: Yes. You can create multiple routes: one pinned to smaller batch windows and a separate route with aggressive batching. Smart routing can send requests to different routes by header or token.

[04:01] Olivia: From a security perspective, if we fallback to hosted, how is data isolation handled? We have PCI concerns.
[04:07] Hannah: Great question. Fallback policies are configurable. For customers with strict residency/compliance, we can disable cross-tenant or cross-region fallback. For VPC/private deployments we can define an internal fallback within the VPC only. If you need absolute isolation, we recommend dedicated-only with reserved capacity bumping or throttling rules to avoid external fallback.
[04:28] Olivia: So hosted fallback would send data out of our VPC?
[04:31] Raj: Only if you enable it. Default enterprise templates keep data within customer-designated regions; hosted fallback still goes through Redwood's hosted clusters but can be restricted — however, for PCI we usually advise against any hosted fallback unless under a strict contract and encryption-in-flight with KMS controls.

[04:48] [05:00]
[05:00] Lina: Can you talk about automatic fallback triggers? I want to know thresholds. Is it based on queue depth, scheduler slowdowns, or measured tail latency?
[05:08] Raj: It's policy-driven. Common triggers: slot OOM events, sustained CPU/GPU utilization above threshold, queue latency > X ms, or sustained KV miss rates. You can pick multiple conditions and a priority order — e.g., first try a local model variant (quantized/no-KV), then route to a smaller model, then region fallback, then hosted.
[05:28] Mark: Smaller model — do you mean a distillation or a quantized variant? How is quality impacted?
[05:32] Raj: Could be either. Quantized variants reduce memory and speed up kernels, but can introduce small deltas in output quality. We recommend running your eval set and Redwood Optimize can produce quality vs latency curves so you can set acceptable boundaries. For many ranking or short-response tasks, int8 quantization gives huge perf wins with minimal quality loss.
[05:50] James: Any metrics you can share? Like p50/p95/p99 deltas for int8 vs fp16?
[05:55] Raj: Rough ballpark — int8 often reduces token latency by 20–35% and decreases memory footprint by ~30–50% depending on model and kernel optimizations. p99 improvements are workload-dependent; if your p99 is KV-miss dominated, quantization helps less. We'll share our microbenchmark numbers.

[06:14] [06:30]
[06:30] Lina: About KV hotpaths — you said you have prefetch heuristics. How adaptive are they? Ours have diurnal patterns and sudden events.
[06:38] Hannah: The heuristics are a mix of LRU with frequency counters and short-term recency windows. For spikes we have a short-term hotset detector that raises prefetch budget for keys with high read-rate. It also signals autoscaler to provision additional slots if hotness persists.
[06:54] Mark: How immediate is that—like seconds or minutes?
[06:57] Raj: Hotset detection is in seconds to tens of seconds. Autoscaling is constrained by underlying GPU provisioning and takes minutes. That's why we recommend combining short-term mitigations (prefetch, throttling less-critical requests) with longer-term capacity actions.

[07:12] Olivia: For on-prem/private, can we plug in our own NVMe pools? We have high-perf local storage.
[07:18] Raj: Yes, Private deployments support customer-supplied NVMe tiers. We can configure the runtime to use local NVMe for the slow-tier KV store, which reduces tail compared to network-attached storage. That often helps a lot with p99.

[07:29] [08:00]
[08:00] James: What about experiments that show eviction storms when a new model is deployed and cache warming hasn't occurred?
[08:06] Hannah: During rollout we recommend canary warmup: spin up canary instances and pre-warm KV for a subset of users, then gradually ramp. We also support a gradual KV migration utility that migrates hot keys to the new pool before traffic is cut over.
[08:21] Lina: Could Redwood's runtime do background prefetch from the old model's cache to new cache?
[08:25] Raj: We have a migration path that pulls most-frequently-used keys and copies them into the target KV namespace prior to full cutover. It's not zero-cost but avoids the immediate cold-start storm.

[08:40] [09:00]
[09:00] Mark: On batching—what's the recommended configuration for payments flows where latency matters but you also want efficiency?
[09:07] Raj: Two-lane approach: an interactive lane with max_batch_time_ms ~ 5–10ms, small max_batch_size; and a background lane with 50–100ms. For session-based KV-dependent flows, keep the interactive lane KV-warmed. Also prefer dynamic batching which groups by sequence length to avoid token padding waste.
[09:27] James: Does dynamic batching increase variance?
[09:29] Raj: Slightly. It increases throughput while keeping average latencies lower, but p99 can be impacted by outlier long sequences in a batch. That's where sequence bucketing helps.

[09:42] [10:00]
[10:00] Lina: How are rate limits and throttles enforced in Dedicated? We need to ensure spikes don't starve other critical paths.
[10:06] Raj: We have multi-layer enforcement: per-token rate limits at the routing layer, per-route concurrency caps, and queue-depth thresholds that trigger backpressure or reject/call-fallback. You can set QoS labels so critical routes get priority.
[10:21] Lina: Can we map enterprise users to higher QoS?
[10:24] Raj: Yes, token-level or API-key-level QoS is supported.

[10:36] [11:00]
[11:00] Olivia: About audits — if we run in Private with KMS, do you provide audit logs of fallbacks? We need that for compliance.
[11:06] Hannah: Yes. Private deployments can ship detailed audit events: routing decision, fallback reason, original request id, and timestamps. We can integrate with your SIEM.
[11:14] Olivia: And KMS?
[11:16] Raj: We support customer-managed KMS/HSM for keys at rest. For hosted fallback we can encrypt payloads with customer keys until they hit Redwood's runtime, but many customers with strict compliance avoid fallback entirely.

[11:30] [12:00]
[12:00] Mark: Let's step through two concrete failure scenarios and answers: 1) sudden KV hot keys and eviction storm; 2) GPU saturation because of long-sequence batch storm.
[12:10] Raj: For (1): short-term — enable prefetch budget increase and route non-critical traffic to background lane; mid-term — spin up an extra slot/pool (autoscaler) and copy hot keys to new pool; long-term — analyze key distribution and consider sharding hot keys across multiple KV namespaces. For (2): we throttle long-seq requests, move them to a different model variant or smaller batch slot, and if necessary route to dedicated overflow pool. We also can reduce max_batch_time_ms dynamically for that pool to reduce queueing.
[12:38] James: What about detection — are these automations pre-built or manual?
[12:41] Raj: You can use Redwood Console policies to automate these actions based on metrics; threshold actions can be auto-triggered or manual with alerts.

[12:54] [13:00]
[13:00] Lina: In a practical runbook, who does what? If SLA is breached, do you automatically spin more GPUs or do we need to approve?
[13:08] Hannah: By default autoscaling is enabled with safe guards to avoid runaway costs. You can set escalation rules: auto-scale up to X nodes, then notify SRE for manual approval beyond that. For Dedicated, reserved capacity contracts may include preapproved burst budgets.

[13:22] Mark: We have reserved capacity now but it's insufficient for traffic spikes. Can Redwood do temporary short-term capacity increases?
[13:28] Raj: Yes, we have burst capacity options that draw from a shared pool for short durations. They need pre-agreement for guaranteed latency; otherwise it's best-effort.

[13:39] [14:00]
[14:00] James: We're concerned about tail latency during holidays when traffic spikes are extreme. Anything special?
[14:06] Raj: For predictable peak events, pre-provision extra dedicated pools and run a warmup. For unpredictable spikes, configure fallback priorities: degrade to smaller model variants rather than failing requests. Also implement early-reject policies for low-priority batch tasks.

[14:22] Lina: Are we able to do synthetic load tests with Redwood to observe p99 behavior?
[14:26] Maya: Yes — we can run a joint benchmark. Raj will set up a harness you can run from your VPC (or from Redwood hosted if you prefer) and we'll collect p50/p95/p99/99.9 and KV miss rates.

[14:40] [15:00]
[15:00] Mark: A quick tangent — quantization: can Redwood do mixed-precision per-layer or is it whole-model?
[15:07] Raj: We support per-layer mixed quantization in our compilation pipeline when it yields better quality. Our Optimize tool can sweep per-layer settings and output recommended profiles.
[15:16] Mark: That could be useful — keep critical attention layers fp16 and quantize middle layers.

[15:23] Olivia: Regarding legal/procurement — if we accept a fallback to hosted, do we need addenda? We need to record that data touched hosted environments.
[15:29] Maya: Typically yes. We add data residency and fallback clauses to contracts. We'll coordinate with your legal.

[15:38] [16:00]
[16:00] James: Any cases where fallback to hosted has been used in production for other customers? How did they manage risk?
[16:05] Raj: We had a fintech customer with seasonal spikes; they used hosted fallback but encrypted payloads with their KMS and had strict SLA tiers with pre-approved burst capacity. They also used canary warmups and pre-warmed caches during peak windows. It worked, but only with careful planning and contract-level guarantees.

[16:23] Lina: One more—what observability will we get? Token-level cost, KV hit rates, per-route latency histos?
[16:29] Hannah: Yes — Redwood Console surfaces token-level cost, per-route p50/p95/p99 histograms, KV hit/miss, cache size and eviction rates, batch sizes, queue depths, and fallback events. You can export to Prometheus/Grafana.

[16:45] [17:00]
[17:00] Mark: Ok let's talk pilot: what minimal data do you need to run the microbenchmark?
[17:06] Raj: Sample prompt corpus (1000–5000 representative requests), average and 95/99 seq-lengths, and some KV access traces if possible. Also expected RPS distribution and peak multipliers.

[17:18] Lina: We'll provide histograms and a 2-week sample of production traces.

[17:22] Maya: Great. We'll produce a benchmark plan and proposed pilot configuration.

[17:28] [18:00]
[18:00] Raj: Quick recap of technical recommendations: 1) Two-lane routing (interactive vs bulk) with sequence bucketing; 2) KV warmup strategies + migration tool during rollouts; 3) Use int8/mixed quant profiles run through Optimize to pick acceptable quality; 4) Autoscale + burst capacity with preapproved thresholds for critical windows; 5) For PCI-sensitive workloads, disable hosted fallback and use Private or dedicated with KMS/HSM.

[18:46] Olivia: That sounds good. We'll need the audit log schema and KMS integration docs.

[18:51] Maya: We'll share both.

[19:00] [19:30]
[19:30] Final Q&A and clarifications — small bits:
- Lina asks about cost delta if we use burst capacity vs disabling fallback — Hannah gives anecdotal numbers: burst adds ~25–40% over steady reserved cost during peaks but avoids fallback and potential compliance overhead.
- Mark requests per-layer quantization report.
- James requests runbook for auto-escalation.

[20:15] Maya: Ok we'll summarize next steps and owners in the follow-up email. Anything else?
[20:20] Mark: No, that's all. Appreciate the technical depth.

[20:28] Meeting end: 2026-03-21 15:54 UTC
